certainty_reasoning: Sox's own wording is unambiguous and repeated: Marshall is 'the love of his life' (p. 37), 'his future lover' (p. 42), 'his great love' (p. 128), 'his beloved (Puppy)' (p. viii), and after the 1889 capitulation letter Sox writes flatly 'John Marshall admitted he was in love' (p. 44). The evidence Sox prints is participant correspondence in the source (drawn, per his pp. ix-x, from the Warren-Marshall letters printed by Burdett & Goddard 1941 and the originals at the Ashmolean): Warren's 1887-89 wooing letters ('take lodgings with me?', 'dine alone with me'), Marshall's 1889 'my love to you' letter, Marshall's 1893 'Puppy dear. Not proposed as documented-sexual: no passage read attests sexual relations in first person - the letters attest love, cohabitation and lifelong partnership; the nearest sexual framings are Warren's authorship of A Defence of Uranian Love (pp. 153-154) and his 'the Museum was truly a paederastic evangel. It must be counted as a result of love' (pp. 128-129), plus Fothergill's 'Ned never touched a woman in his life, nor, perhaps had Marshall' (p. 76), which cuts both ways. Caveat for the owner on the consensus criterion: Sox is the only secondary source read so far; Burdett & Goddard 1941 corroborates the pair-bond in passages Sox quotes ('replicas of each other' p. 39; Ned telling Burdett he had wanted Marshall 'to be buried with me' p. 130) but was not independently read - if two independently-read secondaries are required, this technically sits at single-source until Burdett-Goddard or Martin Green is read; 'alleged' would however misfit a bond that no source read contests. Addendum (p. 21, rendered): analysing Warren's A Tale of Pausanian Love, Sox writes that before they met 'Warren and Marshall were equally inexperienced, and both were very confused regarding their sexuality', and that while Marshall 'was not adverse to the idea of marriage', for Ned 'that course was utterly unthinkable and a betrayal of homosexual idealism' - Sox's most direct statement of the partnership's homosexual-idealist frame.
date_label: Met at New College, Oxford, 1884 (Marshall's third year); Warren's 'protracted wooing' by letter 1887-89; 'Marshall gave in (1889)' and by November 1889 'the man of his choice' was at Ned's side; Lewes House from 1890. Strained from 1906-07: Marshall married Warren's cousin Mary Bliss 5 Nov. 1907 and moved to Rome, still collecting on Warren's subsidy. Sharing their old Rome flat again at the end, Marshall died in Warren's presence, February 1928 ('five minutes past one', night of the 15th, per Warren's account); Warren died 28 December 1928; his ashes joined the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca, 5 April 1929.
summary: The forty-year partnership at the centre of the Lewes House 'brotherhood of aesthetes'. Warren met Marshall at New College in 1884 and wooed him by letter for years - 'I had hoped that usually you would consent to dine alone with me' - until Marshall 'gave in' in 1889 with a letter ending 'everything you say and do seems inseparable from you and my love to you'; Sox adds 'John Marshall admitted he was in love'. They called each other 'Puppy', ran the antiquities-collecting enterprise for Boston from Lewes House, and Sox names Marshall 'the love of his life' and 'his future lover'. Marshall's 1907 marriage to Warren's cousin Mary Bliss - a 'betrayal of their common ideal' to Warren; 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union' per Sox - moved the Marshalls to Rome on Warren's subsidy. Warren was living with Marshall again at his death in February 1928: he kissed him good-night and heard 'good-bye Puppy' several times as Marshall died; ten months later Warren was dead, his ashes placed in the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca under a Grecian urn.

sources.quote: Marshall was at last hooked and wrote to Ned: 'You were to me at first a quality, then a collection of qualities, and at last. well! you were Warren: and now everything you say and do seems inseparable from you and my love to you. That makes my judgement in the matter infallible.' John Marshall admitted he was in love.
sources.context: September 1889: Marshall had presented his conditions for becoming Ned's secretary; Ned answered 'Dear Marechal, your plan of the secretaryship comes near to what I have been wanting for a long time' and, on Marshall's dining-with-the-servants condition, 'I had hoped that usually you would consent to dine alone with me' (p. 43). Two paragraphs after the quote: 'By November 1889, "the man of his choice" was at Ned's side.' The letter runs over the printed 43/44 page break.
sources.supports: Promoted to lead by the Q2 quality pass, displacing Sox's phrase 'the love of his life'. This is the passage in which a participant says most plainly what the bond was: Marshall's own letter ending the two-year courtship, tracing how Warren stopped being a set of qualities and became simply 'Warren', and closing on 'my love to you'. Marshall's letter to Warren, September 1889, as printed by Sox; Sox's flat sentence after it - 'John Marshall admitted he was in love' - is the historian reading the same letter, and is kept inside the quotation so the reader can weigh the two. Partnership begun November 1889.
sources.provenance: PDF pages 59-60, printed folios 43-44 confirmed on rendered pages. Inner '. ' ellipses are as printed.

sources.quote: With Ned Warren love and collecting were inexorably entwined and the extent and direction of that collecting took shape in the context of the love of his life, John Marshall, his 'Puppy'.
sources.context: Closing sentence of Part II ch. 1 ('Why Do Men Collect?'); the preceding sentence quotes Kenneth Clark on collecting being as irrational as falling in love. The Introduction carries the same framing: 'his beloved "Puppy" (as he called John Marshall)' (p. viii).
sources.supports: Sox's class-deciding characterization: Marshall as 'the love of his life'; the 'Puppy' nickname
sources.provenance: PDF page 53, printed folio 37 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: In the letter to Curtius, Ned had also commented on how he viewed his future lover: 'I used to think that he took his tragedy in daily life, and his comedy in literature. He was a man very much preoccupied with his own subjects, and with his own ideas. Sometimes inappreciative of others who did not strike his own fancy, a better judge of art than of people, but unpretentious and very touching in his affections.'
sources.context: 'His future lover' is Sox's own phrase, introducing Warren's much-later letter to the archaeologist Ludwig Curtius about Marshall in the 1889 period. The same page prints the wooing letters: 27 Feb. 1887, 'What will become of our project for travel?. I wonder whether it would amuse you to take lodgings with me?'; and from Bad-Ems, 'Unless I hear from you at once. I shall cast out my lines for other fish whom I see drifting down stream.'
sources.supports: Sox's 'his future lover' wording; the 'numerous and intense' courtship correspondence of 1887-89
sources.provenance: PDF page 58, printed folio 42 confirmed on rendered page. The Curtius letter is undated in the pages read.

sources.quote: From Rome he complained to Ned: 'I feel so weak here; I am rather down - I can do nothing. I go round and round seeing worthless things. I suspect everybody. I am sick of being alone and Puppy dear, it is bad for me. I would sooner do anything than live alone. Do, therefore, if you can, hurry up the business here. I am a bit unhappy.' This is one of the most personal outpourings we have from John Marshall.
sources.context: Marshall alone at the Rome end of the collecting operation. 'Puppy dear' is Marshall addressing Warren - the nickname ran both directions (Warren signs 'Your Puppy' in the 4 May 1914 letter printed at p. 107; the jacket: 'they called each other "Puppy"'). Sox retro-dates the letter at p. 76 as 'this threat of 1893'. Inner '. ' is as printed; the passage crosses the printed 64/65 break.
sources.supports: Participant letter: Marshall's emotional dependence ('I would sooner do anything than live alone'); the mutual 'Puppy' nickname in first-person use
sources.provenance: PDF pages 80-81, printed folios 64-65 confirmed on rendered pages.

sources.quote: 'a middle-aged cousin of Ned's who came to stay with us: she didn't like me, and courted Ned and Marshall, either of which she was well prepared to marry. But Ned never touched a woman in his life, nor, perhaps had Marshall. Naively Mary thought the marriage would unite Johnny more closely to Ned.' … Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union of Mary and John Marshall, but she was an extremely beneficial help-mate in his collecting at the Metropolitan Museum.
sources.context: The first block is Fothergill's memoir describing Mary Bliss, as printed by Sox ('Fothergill described her as.'; the inner '. ' is as printed); the sentence after the elision is Sox's own narration. Same page: 'John Marshall did not marry Ned's cousin until 5 November 1907.' Mary Bliss was Warren's cousin (p. viii); Warren had dedicated The Prince Who Did Not Exist (1900) to her (p. 75).
sources.supports: The marriage as the record frames it: Mary's own hope that it 'would unite Johnny more closely to Ned'; Sox: 'Neither love nor sex had anything to do with the union'; Fothergill on the men's celibacy toward women
sources.provenance: PDF page 92, printed folio 76 confirmed on rendered page. Chain for the first block: Fothergill memoir, as printed in Sox 1991, p. 76.

sources.quote: Ned sensed what was transpiring but, fatalistically, did nothing about it. By the spring of 1907 it became clear that Marshall would marry. Though he told Marshall this was a 'betrayal of their common ideal', Ned said he would stand by his friend 'married or unmarried'.
sources.context: Marshall, often left alone at Lewes while Warren fought his family lawsuit in America, had called Edward Robinson (the Met) and Mary Bliss his 'only loopholes of escape'. Same page: 'Ned seemed so consumed by his new interest in Harry Thomas. that he submerged his feelings for Marshall'; 'After the marriage, however, Ned was as good as his word' - the Rome flat and subsidized income; 'Of the forty years during which Warren knew Marshall, half were after his marriage.' Fothergill's account adds that Ned was reduced to 'frenzied and unreasonable agitation' over the thought of Marshall's marrying (p. 154).
sources.supports: The marriage strain: Warren's 'betrayal of their common ideal' and his standing by Marshall 'married or unmarried'
sources.provenance: PDF page 94, printed folio 78 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: Ned gave a vivid account of his friend's last hours to John Fothergill: 'On the evening of the 15th Johnny went to bed early, say towards nine. … I went to his bed and kissed him good-night; he said that he was going to sleep; usually he read a little in bed. Our rooms were connected by an open door. … he looked wild and said good-bye to the servants and said "good-bye Puppy" several times to me. … In ten minutes he was dead.'
sources.context: February 1928, Rome: 'Marshall returned to Rome, and Ned was there. the two shared a flat they had lived in during their collecting days' (p. 126). The account is a set-off block extract in the original (outer quotation marks added here; 'good-bye Puppy' is in single quotes in the original). It continues: 'I lay on the other side of him propping up his head. I got up and looked at my watch; it was five minutes past one.' Full extract (W16).
sources.supports: Warren's first-person account of Marshall's death: cohabiting again, the good-night kiss, 'good-bye Puppy' as Marshall's last words to him. Read with the burial passage below (p. 130), this is Warren's own answer to what Marshall was to him.
sources.provenance: PDF pages 142-143, printed folios 126-127 confirmed on rendered pages. Chain: Warren letter to Fothergill, as printed in Sox 1991, pp. 126-127.

sources.quote: Ned told Osbert Burdett that he had wanted Marshall 'to be buried with me, but he had made his will just after his wife's death and before he had begun to understand me again.'
sources.context: Sox, in the closing pages on Warren's own death (28 December 1928, ten months after Marshall's); the inner words are Warren's, spoken to his biographer Osbert Burdett. The same page records that Warren's ashes went instead to the Marshalls' tomb at Bagni di Lucca in spring 1929, under a plain Grecian urn bearing the names of Mary and John Marshall and Edward Perry Warren.
sources.supports: Warren's own most explicit claim on the relationship, and the counterpart to Marshall's 1889 avowal at the head of this record: he had wanted to be buried with Marshall. It is a spousal claim made in the one register the law left open to him, and the clause that follows is Warren's account of why it failed - Marshall's will was made in the estrangement after his wife's death, 'before he had begun to understand me again'. Warren to Osbert Burdett, as quoted by Sox.
sources.provenance: PDF page 146 (printed folio 130 confirmed on the rendered page).
